name: litellm

facts.description: The fastest, litest AI Gateway. Rust core with Python SDK. Call 100+ LLM APIs in OpenAI (or native) format with cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing, and logging [Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, OpenAI, VertexAI, vLLM, Nvidia NIM]

title: LiteLLM: An AI Gateway and Python SDK for Multi-Provider LLM Access
answer: LiteLLM is an AI gateway and Python SDK from BerriAI that lets you call over 100 LLM APIs, including OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Azure, VertexAI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM, in OpenAI or native format. It adds cost tracking, guardrails, load balancing, logging and budget controls, and is moving to a Rust core for lower latency and memory. The one thing to know before adopting it is that it sits in the request path, so its incidents and version upgrades directly affect production traffic.

sections.body: LiteLLM is made by BerriAI and is both a Python SDK and a self-hosted gateway, described on its site as the fastest, litest AI Gateway with a Rust core and Python SDK. It appeared as an open source project on GitHub, where it has around 60,090 stars, and its documentation lives at docs.litellm.ai. It serves the routing and control layer of the AI stack, sitting between your application and many model providers. Rather than calling each provider's SDK directly, you send requests through LiteLLM, which normalizes them into OpenAI or native format and applies policy. The repository's last recorded push was October 3, 2026, and the licence is listed as custom, so review terms before commercial use.
sections.heading: What it is and where it sits in AI work

sections.body: The site shows LiteLLM used for calling over 100 LLM APIs, tracking cost, enforcing guardrails, load balancing and logging. Its tutorials cover reliability testing across providers, including batch_completion_models_all_responses, which sends one conversation to every model in parallel and returns only the responses that succeeded, dropping models that raise. It also documents load testing with load_test_model, quality and duration test endpoints, and visualization of results. The gateway handles budgets, rate limits, response caching, usage-based routing and spend tracking, and the Agent Gateway, Model Gateway and MCP Gateway give one control plane for agents, model traffic and tool access. It is strongest where teams need one policy and billing layer across many providers rather than a single vendor SDK.
sections.heading: What it is used for and where it is strongest

sections.body: The Python SDK is approachable for developers who already know Python and basic HTTP APIs, since the site's examples are short and use familiar completion-style calls. The gateway is a larger commitment: you need to understand deployment, Redis, authentication through OIDC or another supported credential, team and key budgets, and rate limiting. The site's incident reports assume you can reason about versions, pre-releases and backports, which is systems knowledge rather than machine learning mathematics. No deep model training background is required, because LiteLLM routes and governs calls rather than training models. The official documentation offers tutorials, a proxy setup path and admin UI material, though the facts here do not show a structured beginner course.
sections.heading: How hard it is to learn and what you need first

sections.body: LiteLLM integrates with a long list of providers including Bedrock, Azure, OpenAI, Anthropic, VertexAI, vLLM and Nvidia NIM, and its site documents an A2A JSON-RPC interface for agents, an MCP Gateway for tool access, and OAuth2 authorization code flow with PKCE for per-user credentials. It supports OIDC authentication, SSO and SAML, audit logs, multi-team management and guardrails. The project has a large GitHub following at roughly 60,090 stars, and its blog carries tags for ai-gateway and incident-report, with posts covering Redis round-trip reductions, a Rust gateway beta, and detailed postmortems. Documentation is extensive, with 60 pages read, but the licence is custom, so community use and commercial use may differ.
sections.heading: Ecosystem and community

sections.body: LiteLLM serves both ends. The Python SDK is quick for experiments, letting you swap providers with small code changes, and the site's batch and load testing helpers support early reliability checks. In production, the Python proxy has known costs: the site says it peaks around 359MB of memory under load, and an incident report describes a customer's worker process reaching 61GB RSS during a Redis outage, with kernel OOM kills and thousands of failed requests. The Rust gateway beta is the answer to that, claiming about 15x throughput, from 453 to 6,782 requests per second, on about 11x less memory, 359MB to 32MB, and per-request overhead near 0.05ms against about 7.5ms on the Python path. The trade is maturity: the Rust gateway is an early beta, while the Python proxy is the established path.
sections.heading: Prototyping speed against production performance

sections.body: The site's material points to enterprise use, including SSO and SAML, audit logs, spend tracking, multi-team management and guardrails built for production, and an incident report describes an enterprise customer running litellm-database:v1.100.0 behind nginx. It also describes a shared-agent deployment with two business units in a shared-agents-team, and finance and payroll tool access restricted by group. That suggests adoption in platform and finops teams that need one control plane across providers. The facts do not name specific public companies or give market share, so claims about being an industry standard would go beyond what is supported. For a career, LiteLLM experience maps to AI platform, gateway and cost governance roles rather than model research, and the project's active release cadence means version awareness is part of the skill.
sections.heading: Industry adoption and careers

sections.body: LiteLLM is written in Python and is typically used from Python applications, though the gateway is language agnostic because clients speak HTTP and OpenAI-compatible formats. It sits beside provider SDKs rather than replacing them, calling Mistral's API directly over HTTP via httpx instead of importing the mistralai package, and it fronts runtimes such as vLLM and Nvidia NIM as well as hosted APIs from OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Azure and VertexAI. It also works with agent protocols, including A2A JSON-RPC and MCP for tools. The polyglot pattern is a Python or other application calling a LiteLLM gateway, which then routes to many backends, with the Rust core taking over hot paths such as auth and rate limiting as that migration completes.
sections.heading: How it fits beside the others

sections.body: The site is candid about failures. A Medium severity incident in v1.100.0 caused kernel OOM kills and a 61GB worker process when provider failures, retries and an unreachable Redis combined, and a silent cost regression in v1.91.0 and v1.91.1 broke Anthropic prompt caching for Claude Code on Bedrock, dropping cache hit rates from roughly 90% to 25-45% and raising spend 2-3x. The Rust gateway is an early beta, so its benchmark claims, including 7x lower overhead and 9x less memory than Bifrost, come from the vendor's own AIGatewayBench and are not independently verified. The licence is custom and the facts do not explain its terms. The site also does not say how the Rust migration will handle every existing feature, or when the Python proxy will be fully superseded.
sections.heading: Limits and open questions
